item.title: Understanding Your Utility Bill: The Complete Guide for 2026
item.description:
Your utility bills arrive every month. You glance at the total, pay it, and move on. But those bills contain valuable information—and possible errors costing you money. Every line item, every charge, every rate structure affects what you pay.

This guide explains electricity, gas, and water bills in plain English. You’ll learn what every charge means, how rate structures work, how to spot errors, and how to lower each type of bill.

item.title: Average utility bills by state: Full Comparison (2026)
item.description:
Quick Answer: Average U.S. Utility Bills in 2026

The average U.S. household pays $430–$500 per month for all utilities combined (electricity, gas, water, sewer, trash). Here is the national breakdown:

  • Electricity: $137/month (≈900 kWh at 14.3¢/kWh)
  • Natural gas: $60–$120/month (higher in winter, lower in summer)
  • Water & sewer: $70–$120/month combined
  • Internet: $60–$80/month
  • Trash/recycling: $15–$35/month (often bundled with water)

The cheapest states for utilities are Idaho, Utah, and Washington (abundant hydropower). The most expensive are Hawaii, Alaska, and Connecticut. For a full state-by-state breakdown, see the tables below. To understand what drives these costs, see our guide on how utility rates, fees, and usage work together.

item.title: Gas Delivery Charge vs Supply Charge: What
item.description:
Quick Answer

# Gas Delivery Charge vs Supply Charge: What's the Difference?

The gas supply charge pays for the actual natural gas molecule you consume, while the gas delivery charge covers the cost of the infrastructure, pipes, and service required to transport that fuel safely to your home. This split is known as "unbundling," and understanding it is the first step to controlling your energy budget. While the supply charge fluctuates based on global market prices, the delivery charge is typically regulated by state public utility commissions and remains more stable, though it can still rise due to infrastructure maintenance or taxes. Most homeowners see both combined on a single line item or separated into two distinct sections, but knowing which part of the bill you can control is essential for saving money.

item.title: How to Read Your Gas Meter: Every Meter Type With Step-by-Step Instructions
item.description:
Quick Answer

**To read your gas meter**, look at the dials or digital display from **left to right** and record the numbers shown. For dial meters, if a pointer is between two numbers, always record the **lower number** and ignore red test dials.

  • Dial meters: Read **left to right** (opposite of electric meters), record lower number when pointer is between digits
  • Digital/smart meters: Simply read the number displayed on screen—usually in **CCF** (hundred cubic feet) or **therms**

Track your usage to spot [billing errors](/blog/12-how-to-read-your-gas-bill) and potential gas leaks.

item.title: MCF vs CCF vs Therms on Your Gas Bill: What the Units Actually Mean
item.description:
Quick Answer

# MCF vs CCF vs Therms on Your Gas Bill: What the Units Actually Mean

Therms measure the actual heat energy you use, while CCF and MCF measure the physical volume of gas flowing through your meter. To compare costs accurately, you must convert these volume units into therms because gas density varies by region and temperature. Understanding MCF vs CCF vs therms on gas bill is essential for spotting billing errors, comparing utility rates, and tracking your true energy consumption.

item.title: Why Is My Gas Bill So High in Summer? It
item.description:
Quick Answer

**Your gas bill is high in summer** because of hot water heating (**18-20% of home energy use**), gas clothes dryers running longer in humid weather, outdoor appliances like pool heaters (**$50-$150/month extra**), or billing errors from estimated meter readings.

  • Water heating is the #1 summer culprit: Showers, laundry, and dishes account for **40-50% of summer gas usage** when heating is off
  • Pool heaters are extremely expensive: They can add **$50-$150 per month** to your bill during swim season

Learn how to [detect gas leaks](/blog/12-how-to-read-your-gas-bill) and verify meter readings to resolve high bills.

item.title: Why Is My Gas Bill So High in Winter? The Real Reasons (and Fixes)
item.description:
Quick Answer

**Your gas bill is high in winter** because your heating system works harder in cold weather, gas rates often spike during peak demand, and billing cycles may include more days. Winter bills can reach **$200-$400 per month** compared to **$50-$100 in summer**—a **300-400% increase**.

  • Primary driver: Cold temperatures force your furnace to run longer, consuming **2-3x more therms** than summer months
  • Rate spikes: Gas prices can jump **22% higher** during winter due to market demand

Check your [thermostat settings](/blog/05-how-to-lower-utility-bills) and seal air leaks to reduce costs.

item.title: Gas Customer Charge Explained (Why You Pay Even With Low Usage)
item.description:
The problem: you used very little gas, but the bill still arrived

Many people cut usage in summer and expect the bill to drop close to zero. Then the statement shows a steady monthly charge anyway.

That line is usually the customer charge (also called a basic service charge). It is standard on most gas bills, and it does not depend on therms used.

Table of contents

  • The short answer
  • What the customer charge covers
  • Why it does not go away
  • Where to find it on the bill
  • How it affects bill comparisons
  • Customer charge vs supply vs delivery
  • Common misconceptions
  • FAQs

The short answer

The customer charge is a fixed monthly fee that keeps your gas service active. It helps cover meter service, billing, and the infrastructure needed to deliver gas safely.
